We maintain a continuously updated project at: https://github.com/digailab/awesome-llm-implicit-reasoning.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought from the Hopfieldian View
papers.research_question: How does the reasoning capability emerge through Chain-of-Thought prompting? The paper aims to explain the fundamental factors behind CoT's success.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hopfieldian view of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, connecting it to cognitive neuroscience, and proposes the Representation-of-Thought framework to enhance robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a Hopfieldian framework for CoT interpretability, introducing error localization and the RoT framework, which improves robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Hopfieldian view provides a framework to understand CoT reasoning as movement between representation spaces.
A method for localizing reasoning errors in CoT responses is developed based on low-dimensional representation spaces.
The Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework enhances the robustness of CoT reasoning by manipulating hidden states towards representation spaces.
Experimental results show RoT improves accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.
RoT offers fine-grained control over the reasoning process and improves interpretability.
future_direction: Exploring other elements of the Hopfieldian view such as attractors and state space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various tasks, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting emerging as a key technique to enhance reasoning capabilities. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving performance, lacking a comprehensive framework to explain and understand the fundamental factors behind CoT's success. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel perspective grounded in the Hopfieldian view of cognition in cognitive neuroscience. We establish a connection between CoT reasoning and key cognitive elements such as stimuli, actions, neural populations, and representation spaces. From our view, we can understand the reasoning process as the movement between these representation spaces. Building on this insight, we develop a method for localizing reasoning errors in the response of CoTs. Moreover, we propose the Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework, which leverages the robustness of low-dimensional representation spaces to enhance the robustness of the reasoning process in CoTs. Experimental results demonstrate that RoT improves the robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning while offering fine-grained control over the reasoning process.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: An Investigation of Neuron Activation as a Unified Lens to Explain Chain-of-Thought Eliciting Arithmetic Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can neuron activation in feed-forward layers of LLMs provide a unified explanation for the importance of various components in Chain-of-Thought prompts for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that analyzing the activation of reasoning neurons in feed-forward layers provides a unified explanation for why certain components (e.g., equations, textual explanation) in Chain-of-Thought prompts are important for eliciting arithmetic reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Neuron activation analysis provides valuable insights into the internal mechanism of LLMs for arithmetic reasoning and can explain prior empirical observations about Chain-of-Thought prompting.
papers.key_findings:
The paper discovered 113 neurons in Llama2-7B associated with arithmetic reasoning concepts such as logical connectors and arithmetic operations.
Corrupting the discovered reasoning neurons via random noise ablation leads to a significant performance drop, demonstrating their importance for eliciting reasoning.
The presence of equations and textual explanation in CoT prompts leads to higher activation of reasoning neurons, explaining their importance for performance.
Diversity of arithmetic operators in prompts leads to activation of a broader set of reasoning neurons, which improves model performance.
Incorrect in-distribution labels do not substantially affect reasoning neuron activation, while out-of-distribution labels cause different activation patterns and lower performance.
papers.limitation:
Neuron activation is necessary but not sufficient to completely explain LLM reasoning; interactions among components are also important.
The seven pre-defined concepts used may not cover the full scope of arithmetic reasoning, and activation can be faked by prompting.
Analysis was performed primarily on Llama2-7B; generalization to other LLMs may require different approaches.
future_direction: Future work should combine neuron activation analysis with other approaches like circuit analysis and top-down methods for a more complete understanding.
Extend the research to other LLMs and more comprehensive sets of reasoning concepts.
Systematically explore the potential of predicting LLM reasoning performance via neuron activation without human labels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong arithmetic reasoning capabilities when prompted with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts. However, we have only a limited understanding of how they are processed by LLMs. To demystify it, prior work has primarily focused on ablating different components in the CoT prompt and empirically observing their resulting LLM performance change. Yet, the reason why these components are important to LLM reasoning is not explored. To fill this gap, in this work, we investigate ``neuron activation'' as a lens to provide a unified explanation to observations made by prior work. Specifically, we look into neurons within the feed-forward layers of LLMs that may have activated their arithmetic reasoning capabilities, using Llama2 as an example. To facilitate this investigation, we also propose an approach based on GPT-4 to automatically identify neurons that imply arithmetic reasoning. Our analyses revealed that the activation of reasoning neurons in the feed-forward layers of an LLM can explain the importance of various components in a CoT prompt, and future research can extend it for a more complete understanding.

papers.title: Dynamics Within Latent Chain-of-Thought: An Empirical Study of Causal Structure
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three key questions about latent chain-of-thought: (1) which steps are causally necessary for correctness and when answers become decidable early; (2) how influence propagates across steps and how this structure compares to explicit CoT; (3) whether intermediate trajectories retain competing answer modes and how output-level commitment differs from representational commitment across steps.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides the first causal, step-resolved evaluation of latent CoT, showing that latent-step budgets function as staged interfaces with non-local routing and that there is a gap between early output bias and late representational commitment.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that latent-step budgets should be treated as an allocatable interface rather than homogeneous extra depth, and that improving latent reasoning requires shaping routing and commitment rather than simply adding more steps.
papers.key_findings:
Step-wise necessity is heterogeneous: intervening on different latent steps yields different flip rates, indicating unequal causal leverage.
Early-stop decoding shows that correctness becomes decodable at different steps for different tasks and models.
Influence propagation in latent CoT is non-local, with skip connections dominating, unlike explicit CoT which is more chain-like.
Intermediate latent trajectories can retain superposition of competing answer modes, with a gap between output-level commitment and representational commitment.
Coconut models show larger flip rates than CODI, and stronger backbones suppress flips but do not erase step-dependent patterns.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to single-step edits, a fixed latent budget (T=6), and a confined set of paradigms (Coconut/CODI), backbones, and benchmarks.
future_direction: Improving latent reasoning by explicitly shaping where information is written and how it is consolidated across steps (e.g., encouraging stable bottlenecks or controllable routing).
Broader evaluation across more paradigms, longer horizons, and varied intervention types.
papers.abstract: Latent or continuous chain-of-thought methods replace explicit textual rationales with a number of internal latent steps, but these intermediate computations are difficult to evaluate beyond correlation-based probes. In this paper, we view latent chain-of-thought as a manipulable causal process in representation space by modeling latent steps as variables in a structural causal model (SCM) and analyzing their effects through step-wise $\mathrm{do}$-interventions. We study two representative paradigms (i.e., Coconut and CODI) on both mathematical and general reasoning tasks to investigate three key questions: (1) which steps are causally necessary for correctness and when answers become decidable early; (2) how does influence propagate across steps, and how does this structure compare to explicit CoT; and (3) do intermediate trajectories retain competing answer modes, and how does output-level commitment differ from representational commitment across steps. We find that latent-step budgets behave less like homogeneous extra depth and more like staged functionality with non-local routing, and we identify a persistent gap between early output bias and late representational commitment. These results motivate mode-conditional and stability-aware analyses -- and corresponding training/decoding objectives -- as more reliable tools for interpreting and improving latent reasoning systems.

papers.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does this paper investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their internal states through concept injection experiments.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited but functional introspective awareness, which is unreliable but may improve with model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models can detect and identify injected concepts in their activations.
Models can distinguish between injected thoughts and text inputs.
Models can use introspection to detect artificially prefilled outputs.
Models can modulate their internal representations when instructed to think about concepts.
Introspective capabilities are more pronounced in more capable models like Claude Opus 4 and 4.1.
papers.limitation:
The abilities observed are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
Experiments do not pin down specific mechanistic explanations.
Concept injection places models in an unnatural setting.
future_direction: Identifying metacognitive representations more clearly
Investigating the grounding of emotional responses in introspective reports
Exploring introspective capabilities in more natural conditions
papers.abstract: We investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states. It is difficult to answer this question through conversation alone, as genuine introspection cannot be distinguished from confabulations. Here, we address this challenge by injecting representations of known concepts into a model's activations, and measuring the influence of these manipulations on the model's self-reported states. We find that models can, in certain scenarios, notice the presence of injected concepts and accurately identify them. Models demonstrate some ability to recall prior internal representations and distinguish them from raw text inputs. Strikingly, we find that some models can use their ability to recall prior intentions in order to distinguish their own outputs from artificial prefills. In all these experiments, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, the most capable models we tested, generally demonstrate the greatest introspective awareness; however, trends across models are complex and sensitive to post-training strategies. Finally, we explore whether models can explicitly control their internal representations, finding that models can modulate their activations when instructed or incentivized to "think about" a concept. Overall, our results indicate that current language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their own internal states. We stress that in today's models, this capacity is highly unreliable and context-dependent; however, it may continue to develop with further improvements to model capabilities.

papers.title: Distributional reasoning in LLMs: Parallel reasoning processes in multi-hop reasoning
papers.research_question: What strategy does an LLM use to solve multi-hop reasoning questions when not explicitly writing down a thought process (i.e., without chain-of-thought)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that during multi-hop reasoning, LLMs internally activate a distribution of potential intermediate answers in middle layers, and the final answer can be approximated via a linear transformation from this distribution, revealing parallel reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a distributional reasoning process for multi-hop questions, characterized by parallel activation of intermediate possibilities and a linear transformation to final answers, bridging associative and propositional reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The activation vector of potential final answers (A2) can be linearly approximated from the activation vector of potential intermediate answers (A1) extracted from middle layers, with R^2 > 0.5 on average.
Middle layers generate highly interpretable embeddings representing a set of potential intermediate answers, followed by a phase transition where A1 activations decrease and A2 activations increase.
High Spearman correlation exists between the order of top-activated A1 logits in middle layers and their corresponding A2 logits in the output layer.
The same distributional reasoning process occurs even when the model hallucinates answers (on fictitious subjects or out-of-distribution attributes).
The reasoning process is largely handled at the final token position after the middle layers, with minimal influence from other token positions.
papers.limitation:
The questions have a similar general structure; altering the structure could lead to different results.
Different prompt structures, question types, or subjects could lead the model to employ various solving strategies.
The analysis cannot account for semantic categories that lack clear representative tokens (e.g., years).
The statistical analyses do not show direct causality.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for semantic categories lacking clear representative tokens.
Investigate direct causality in the observed process.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to perform tasks believed to require thought processes. When the model does not document an explicit thought process, it becomes difficult to understand the processes occurring within its hidden layers and to determine if these processes can be referred to as reasoning. We introduce a novel and interpretable analysis of internal multi-hop reasoning processes in LLMs. We demonstrate that the prediction process for compositional reasoning questions can be modeled using a simple linear transformation between two semantic category spaces. We show that during inference, the middle layers of the network generate highly interpretable embeddings that represent a set of potential intermediate answers for the multi-hop question. We use statistical analyses to show that a corresponding subset of tokens is activated in the model's output, implying the existence of parallel reasoning paths. These observations hold true even when the model lacks the necessary knowledge to solve the task. Our findings can help uncover the strategies that LLMs use to solve reasoning tasks, offering insights into the types of thought processes that can emerge from artificial intelligence. Finally, we also discuss the implication of cognitive modeling of these results.

papers.title: Eliciting Chain-of-Thought in Base LLMs via Gradient-Based Representation Optimization
papers.research_question: Can we solely manipulate the hidden states to elicit CoT reasoning from a base LLM, without distorting its language quality?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a gradient-based hidden state optimization method to elicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning in base LLMs, using a balanced likelihood and prior regularization framework to guide hidden states toward reasoning while preserving language quality.
papers.conclusion: Presents a principled gradient-based activation optimization method to elicit CoT reasoning from base LLMs, grounded in probabilistic generation theory, which balances likelihood and prior terms to activate reasoning without distribution shift, and consistently outperforms vector arithmetic methods.
papers.key_findings:
Our method consistently outperforms existing hidden state steering methods across diverse reasoning benchmarks.
The method unlocks latent reasoning capabilities in base LLMs without additional training.
The optimization framework balances reasoning effectiveness and linguistic fluency.
The method is effective across multiple LLM architectures (Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, Phi).
The method's performance depends on the choice of hidden states and layers, with middle layers showing better classification performance.
papers.limitation:
The method can only unlock intrinsic reasoning abilities and cannot inject new capabilities; for models with limited intrinsic reasoning capacity, it cannot create non-existent capabilities.
The method's effectiveness depends on the classification performance and layer selection; improper choices may lead to suboptimal results.
future_direction: Integrating the method with post-training techniques to further amplify reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is a critical capability for large language models (LLMs), enabling them to tackle com- plex multi-step tasks. While base LLMs, pre-trained on general text corpora, often struggle with reasoning due to a lack of specialized training, recent studies reveal their latent reason- ing potential tied to hidden states. However, existing hidden state manipulation methods, such as linear activation steering, suffer from limitations due to their rigid and unconstrained nature, often leading to distribution shifts and degraded text quality. In this work, we propose a novel approach for elic- iting CoT reasoning from base LLMs through hidden state manipulation grounded in probabilistic conditional generation. By reformulating the challenge as an optimization problem with a balanced likelihood and prior regularization framework, our method guides hidden states toward reasoning-oriented trajectories while preserving linguistic coherence. Extensive evaluations across mathematical, commonsense, and logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our approach con- sistently outperforms existing steering methods, offering a theoretically principled and effective solution for enhancing reasoning capabilities in base LLMs.

papers.title: Explainable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: An Empirical Analysis on State-Aware Reasoning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can we abstract and model the latent structure of chain-of-thought reasoning to provide a global, explainable view of reasoning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a state-aware transition framework that abstracts chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories into structured latent dynamics via spectral analysis and Markov chains, enabling a global, explainable view of reasoning steps and transitions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a global perspective on multi-step reasoning in LLMs, uncovering consistent latent structures across models and tasks, and enables explainability applications for CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully abstracts CoT reasoning steps into semantically coherent latent states via spectral embeddings and clustering.
Learned transition patterns are consistent across models and tasks, indicating structured reasoning dynamics beyond surface token sequences.
The latent states correspond to meaningful functional roles (e.g., scenario description, problem framing, answer synthesis).
The Markov chain model captures coherent temporal reasoning flows, validated by Monte Carlo simulations.
The approach enables explainability applications such as semantic role identification and temporal pattern visualization.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes access to internal representations of open-source language models.
It focuses primarily on intrinsic structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting have enabled large language models (LLMs) to perform multi-step reasoning. However, the explainability of such reasoning remains limited, with prior work primarily focusing on local token-level attribution, such that the high-level semantic roles of reasoning steps and their transitions remain underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a state-aware transition framework that abstracts CoT trajectories into structured latent dynamics. Specifically, to capture the evolving semantics of CoT reasoning, each reasoning step is represented via spectral analysis of token-level embeddings and clustered into semantically coherent latent states. To characterize the global structure of reasoning, we model their progression as a Markov chain, yielding a structured and interpretable view of the reasoning process. This abstraction supports a range of analyses, including semantic role identification, temporal pattern visualization, and consistency evaluation.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the language model perform multi-step reasoning by recalling memorized information or by following a step-by-step reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that language models perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning tree information can often be detected from attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that encode reasoning information degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with better accuracy and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The work considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
Analysis of multi-head attention is limited; shallow models with many heads might have different head functions.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that language models (LMs) have strong multi-step (i.e., procedural) reasoning capabilities. However, it is unclear whether LMs perform these tasks by cheating with answers memorized from pretraining corpus, or, via a multi-step reasoning mechanism. In this paper, we try to answer this question by exploring a mechanistic interpretation of LMs for multi-step reasoning tasks. Concretely, we hypothesize that the LM implicitly embeds a reasoning tree resembling the correct reasoning process within it. We test this hypothesis by introducing a new probing approach (called MechanisticProbe) that recovers the reasoning tree from the model's attention patterns. We use our probe to analyze two LMs: GPT-2 on a synthetic task (k-th smallest element), and LLaMA on two simple language-based reasoning tasks (ProofWriter & AI2 Reasoning Challenge). We show that MechanisticProbe is able to detect the information of the reasoning tree from the model's attentions for most examples, suggesting that the LM indeed is going through a process of multi-step reasoning within its architecture in many cases.

papers.title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like intuitive reasoning errors, and how do more advanced models avoid these errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs exhibit human-like intuitive errors (System 1), but more advanced models (ChatGPT, GPT-4) avoid these errors through chain-of-thought reasoning and well-developed intuition, performing hyperrationally.
papers.conclusion: Psychological methods can reveal emergent traits in LLMs; advanced LLMs show remarkable reasoning abilities and can avoid intuitive errors, resembling both System 1 and System 2 processes.
papers.key_findings:
Early/smaller LLMs (up to GPT-3-curie) often give atypical responses, indicating poor task comprehension.
Larger pre-ChatGPT models (GPT-3-davinci family) show a high tendency to give intuitive but incorrect responses, similar to human System 1 errors.
ChatGPT models (especially GPT-4) show a high fraction of correct responses, often using chain-of-thought reasoning.
Instructing GPT-3-davinci-003 to use chain-of-thought reasoning reduces intuitive errors and increases correct responses.
Providing training examples (few-shot) improves GPT-3-davinci-003's performance on both CRT and semantic illusions.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested one family of LLMs (the GPT family).
The tasks used are limited in scope (CRT and semantic illusions).
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs is not truly deliberate System 2 reasoning but resembles it.
papers.abstract: We design a battery of semantic illusions and cognitive reflection tests, aimed to elicit intuitive yet erroneous responses. We administer these tasks, traditionally used to study reasoning and decision-making in humans, to OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer model family. The results show that as the models expand in size and linguistic proficiency they increasingly display human-like intuitive system 1 thinking and associated cognitive errors. This pattern shifts notably with the introduction of ChatGPT models, which tend to respond correctly, avoiding the traps embedded in the tasks. Both ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 utilize the input-output context window to engage in chain-of-thought reasoning, reminiscent of how people use notepads to support their system 2 thinking. Yet, they remain accurate even when prevented from engaging in chain-of-thought reasoning, indicating that their system-1-like next-word generation processes are more accurate than those of older models. Our findings highlight the value of applying psychological methodologies to study large language models, as this can uncover previously undetected emergent characteristics.

papers.title: Attention Heads of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of research on attention heads in large language models, introducing a novel four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) to categorize attention head functions and summarizing experimental methods for discovering such heads.
papers.conclusion: The survey consolidates research on attention heads in LLMs, providing a framework for understanding their functions and the methods used to discover them, while highlighting the need for further work on complex tasks, unified frameworks, alignment with human cognition, generalizability, multi-collaboration, and theoretical support.
papers.key_findings:
The paper proposes a four-stage framework (Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, Expression Preparation) inspired by human thought to categorize the functions of attention heads in LLMs.
It provides a detailed taxonomy of special attention heads, categorizing them by their roles in the four stages and the LLM architectures where they were discovered.
The survey summarizes experimental methodologies for discovering attention heads into two main categories: Modeling-Free (Modification-Based and Replacement-Based) and Modeling-Required (Training-Required and Training-Free).
It describes how attention heads collaborate across different stages to solve complex tasks, using the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task as an example.
The paper outlines current limitations in the field, such as a focus on simple tasks and lack of unified frameworks, and proposes future research directions.
papers.limitation:
Current research primarily focuses on simple tasks, leaving complex reasoning tasks underexplored.
There is a lack of unified frameworks to comprehensively describe the mechanisms of attention heads.
Aligning LLM mechanisms with human cognitive processes remains a significant challenge.
future_direction: Extending research to more complex tasks and real-world applications.
Developing unified frameworks to comprehensively describe attention head mechanisms.
Enhancing alignment between LLM mechanisms and human cognitive processes.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of ChatGPT, Large Language Models (LLMs) have excelled in various tasks but remain as black-box systems. Understanding the reasoning bottlenecks of LLMs has become a critical challenge, as these limitations are deeply tied to their internal architecture. Among these, attention heads have emerged as a focal point for investigating the underlying mechanics of LLMs. In this survey, we aim to demystify the internal reasoning processes of LLMs by systematically exploring the roles and mechanisms of attention heads. We first introduce a novel four-stage framework inspired by the human thought process: Knowledge Recalling, In-Context Identification, Latent Reasoning, and Expression Preparation. Using this framework, we comprehensively review existing research to identify and categorize the functions of specific attention heads. Additionally, we analyze the experimental methodologies used to discover these special heads, dividing them into two categories: Modeling-Free and Modeling-Required methods. We further summarize relevant evaluation methods and benchmarks. Finally, we discuss the limitations of current research and propose several potential future directions.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Do Latent Tokens Think? A Causal and Adversarial Analysis of Chain-of-Continuous-Thought
papers.research_question: Do latent tokens in Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT) actually encode reasoning, or do they merely simulate the appearance of it?
papers.core_contribution: Latent tokens in COCONUT function as uninterpretable placeholders and promote shortcut usage, rather than encoding faithful reasoning, leading to inflated benchmark performance without true reasoning.
papers.conclusion: COCONUT tokens serve as pseudo-reasoning placeholders, are not semantically interpretable, and exhibit shortcut behaviors, indicating that latent reasoning in COCONUT is not faithful.
papers.key_findings:
COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering perturbations (PSR <5%) compared to CoT tokens (PSR up to 50%), indicating they lack reasoning-critical information.
Token-swapping experiments show COCONUT's accuracy remains stable after swapping, while CoT's drops, indicating latent tokens have limited influence on final predictions.
COCONUT exhibits strong shortcut dependence, e.g., in MMLU with biased options, incorrect predictions selecting the biased option rise to 70%.
In HotpotQA, COCONUT shows extreme sensitivity to shortcut manipulation, with accuracy dropping to near 0% when shortcuts favor incorrect answers.
PCA visualizations show latent token embeddings are distributed far from the main vocabulary manifold, indicating they act as placeholders without semantic meaning.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not establish a formal causal link between latent representations and reasoning quality.
The study did not deeply investigate the reasons why COCONUT relies on shortcuts, so the analysis remains speculative.
future_direction: Investigate more challenging out-of-distribution evaluations.
Design reasoning-specialized LLM baselines.
Develop novel interpretability metrics to probe latent reasoning traces.
papers.abstract: Latent tokens are gaining attention for enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet their internal mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the problem from a reliability perspective, uncovering fundamental weaknesses: latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders rather than encoding faithful reasoning. While resistant to perturbation, they promote shortcut usage over genuine reasoning. We focus on Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT), which claims better efficiency and stability than explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) while maintaining performance. We investigate this through two complementary approaches. First, steering experiments perturb specific token subsets, namely COCONUT and explicit CoT. Unlike CoT tokens, COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering and lack reasoning-critical information. Second, shortcut experiments evaluate models under biased and out-of-distribution settings. Results on MMLU and HotpotQA demonstrate that COCONUT consistently exploits dataset artifacts, inflating benchmark performance without true reasoning. These findings reposition COCONUT as a pseudo-reasoning mechanism: it generates plausible traces that conceal shortcut dependence rather than faithfully representing reasoning processes.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: MARCOS: Deep Thinking by Markov Chain of Continuous Thoughts
papers.research_question: How can we re-imagine reasoning in large language models to overcome the drawbacks of token-based chain-of-thought, such as slow inference, information bottleneck, and entangled thinking and speaking?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MARCOS, a new paradigm that models reasoning as a Markov chain of continuous thoughts, decoupling thinking from speaking, which achieves performance comparable to or better than token-based chain-of-thought with significant inference speedup.
papers.conclusion: MARCOS presents a new paradigm for latent thinking in LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art reasoning performance and efficiency, while enabling step-level control over randomness and opening avenues for reinforcement learning and non-autoregressive decoding.
papers.key_findings:
MARCOS outperforms all continuous reasoning baselines and surpasses token-based CoT by 4.7% on GSM8K with up to 15.7x inference speedup.
The random variable R_k controls different aspects of reasoning, such as output length and format, without compromising accuracy.
MARCOS supports non-autoregressive decoding in the speaking stage, maintaining competitive accuracy.
Ablation studies show that deep thinking neurons, random variables, and sparsity loss are all critical components.
The model generalizes well to out-of-domain benchmarks like SVAMP and MultiArith.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily focus on mathematical reasoning tasks.
Evaluation is conducted on relatively basic mathematical problems rather than more challenging datasets like MATH or AIME.
The model is trained from scratch and lacks pretraining on massive corpora, limiting its broader capabilities.
future_direction: Develop a pretraining methodology for MARCOS on large, unstructured corpora.
Explore reinforcement learning algorithms that leverage step-level control over randomness for efficient exploration.
Integrate more advanced non-autoregressive decoding strategies to further accelerate inference.
papers.abstract: The current paradigm for reasoning in large language models (LLMs) involves models "thinking out loud" via a sequence of tokens, known as chain-of-thought (CoT). This approach, while effective, has several significant drawbacks. Firstly, inference requires autoregressive generation of often thousands of CoT tokens, which is slow and computationally expensive. Secondly, it constrains reasoning to the discrete space of tokens, creating an information bottleneck across reasoning steps. Thirdly, it fundamentally entangles reasoning with token generation, forcing LLMs to "think while speaking," which causes potentially short-sighted reasoning. In light of these limitations, we re-imagine reasoning in LLMs and present a new paradigm: MARCOS. In our approach, rather than autoregressively generating tokens, we model reasoning as a hidden Markov chain of continuous, high-dimensional "thoughts". Each reasoning step involves a transition of the internal thoughts, where explicit reasoning steps (which may consist of hundreds of tokens) serve as observable variables, which are windows to peek into the implicit thoughts. Since this latent process is incompatible with the standard supervised learning, we further propose a two-phase variational training scheme. Our experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MARCOS outperforms existing continuous reasoning methods and, for the first time, achieves performance comparable to token-based CoT, even surpassing it by 4.7% on GSM8K with up to 15.7x speedup in inference. Beyond this, MARCOS offers additional advantages, such as step-level instead of token-level control over randomness, opening significant opportunities for reinforcement learning and reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Reasoning aligns language models to human cognition
papers.research_question: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do? And if so, what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an active probabilistic reasoning task that disentangles sampling from inference, and a mechanistic model with four latent cognitive variables, showing that chain-of-thought reasoning improves inference quality and shifts LLMs toward human-like decision strategies.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning shifts language models toward human-like evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
Extended reasoning (chain-of-thought) is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference quality while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling.
Reasoning shifts LLMs toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference.
LLMs with extended reasoning can match or exceed humans in inference quality but still underperform in sampling quality compared to skilled humans.
A mechanistic model with four interpretable latent variables (Memory, Strategy, Choice Bias, Occlusion Awareness) captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior and places humans and models in a shared cognitive space.
The model fits reveal that chain-of-thought reasoning reduces inference loss and partially aligns sampling strategies, but a gap in information acquisition remains.
papers.abstract: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do, and what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process? We introduce an active probabilistic reasoning task that cleanly separates sampling (actively acquiring evidence) from inference (integrating evidence toward a decision). Benchmarking humans and a broad set of contemporary large language models against near-optimal reference policies reveals a consistent pattern: extended reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference and producing belief trajectories that become strikingly human-like, while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling. To explain these differences, we fit a mechanistic model that captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior via four interpretable latent variables: memory, strategy, choice bias, and occlusion awareness. This model places humans and models in a shared low-dimensional cognitive space, reproduces behavioral signatures across agents, and shows how chain-of-thought shifts language models toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.

papers.title: Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm uses the elicitation of step-by-step rationales as a proxy for reasoning, gradually refining the model's latent representation of a solution. However, it remains unclear just how early a Large Language Model (LLM) internally commits to an eventual outcome. We probe this by training linear classifiers on hidden states after the first t reasoning tokens, showing that eventual correctness is highly predictable after only a few tokens, even when longer outputs are needed to reach a definite answer. We show that, for harder questions, a drop in predictive accuracy highlights a selection artifact: hard items are disproportionately represented in long CoTs. Overall, our results imply that for reasoning models, internal self-assessment of success tends to emerge after only a few tokens, with implications for interpretability and for inference-time control.

papers.title: Thinking About Thinking: SAGE-nano's Inverse Reasoning for Self-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to introspect on and explain their own reasoning processes, specifically why they choose particular reasoning chains over alternatives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces inverse reasoning, a paradigm enabling LLMs to introspect on their own reasoning processes via attention pathway reconstruction, and presents SAGE-nano, a 4B-parameter model that demonstrates this capability, improving both reasoning transparency and performance.
papers.conclusion: The inverse reasoning paradigm enables LLMs to introspect on their reasoning and generate interpretable explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness while maintaining competitive performance, establishing foundations for transparent AI systems in safety, education, and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE-nano achieves competitive reasoning accuracy (e.g., 74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and high explanation quality (92.1% human preference score).
Inverse reasoning enhances both reasoning transparency and forward reasoning performance, as shown by ablation studies.
The model demonstrates superior introspection accuracy in identifying decision points, alternative paths, and confidence calibration.
The architecture can be trained and deployed efficiently on consumer hardware (Mac Mini M1 cluster), making advanced reasoning more accessible.
Inverse reasoning addresses critical AI safety challenges by providing interpretable explanations of model decision-making.
papers.limitation:
The inverse reasoning approach adds significant computational overhead (40% inference time), limiting scalability to larger models.
Current metrics for explanation quality rely heavily on subjective human evaluation; developing automated evaluation metrics remains an open problem.
Inverse reasoning explanations lack objective ground truth, making validation difficult.
The 4-billion parameter constraint limits the model's capacity for complex reasoning tasks compared to larger state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Investigating inverse reasoning capabilities in larger model architectures (scalability studies).
Extending inverse reasoning to visual and multi-modal reasoning tasks.
Developing robust automated metrics for explanation quality assessment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities at solving complex reasoning tasks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but their decision-making processes remain somewhat blackbox. We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Back Attention: Understanding and Enhancing Multi-Hop Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning, and how can this ability be enhanced?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces back attention, a novel mechanism that allows lower layers to capture higher-layer hidden states, enhancing multi-hop reasoning in LLMs. Also introduces logit flow, an interpretability method for tracing logit propagation.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides new insights into multi-hop reasoning mechanisms and introduces back attention, a powerful and lightweight method that significantly enhances reasoning accuracy in LLMs by allowing lower layers to access higher-layer features.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies four distinct stages in single-hop knowledge prediction: entity subject enrichment, entity attribute extraction, relation subject enrichment, and relation attribute extraction.
Finds that failures in multi-hop reasoning often stem from the relation attribute extraction stage, where conflicting logits reduce prediction accuracy.
Proposes back attention, which enables a 1-layer transformer to achieve the performance of a 2-layer transformer on arithmetic tasks.
Back attention, when fine-tuned on a single layer of pre-trained LLMs, significantly improves accuracy across five reasoning datasets and four different models.
Logit flow provides a neuron-level perspective on information flow, offering a more granular understanding than layer-level methods like activation patching.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability analysis primarily focuses on single-hop and two-hop knowledge queries, which represent specific reasoning scenarios; other reasoning tasks might involve different mechanisms.
Back attention is applied to only a single layer in this work, though it could be extended to two or more layers for potentially greater improvements.
future_direction: Extend back attention to two or more layers.
Validate the findings on more diverse reasoning tasks to refine the interpretability framework for broader applicability.
papers.abstract: We investigate how large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning in prompts like "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's mother's spouse is". To analyze this process, we introduce logit flow, an interpretability method that traces how logits propagate across layers and positions toward the final prediction. Using logit flow, we identify four distinct stages in single-hop knowledge prediction: (A) entity subject enrichment, (B) entity attribute extraction, (C) relation subject enrichment, and (D) relation attribute extraction. Extending this analysis to multi-hop reasoning, we find that failures often stem from the relation attribute extraction stage, where conflicting logits reduce prediction accuracy. To address this, we propose back attention, a novel mechanism that enables lower layers to leverage higher-layer hidden states from different positions during attention computation. With back attention, a 1-layer transformer achieves the performance of a 2-layer transformer. Applied to four LLMs, back attention improves accuracy on five reasoning datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing latent multi-hop reasoning ability.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access".
